tp.step1.detail: Select your biomass feedstock and thermochemical conditions. Temperature (300–900°C), residence time, and heating rate collectively determine the structure of the resulting biochar. Higher temperatures increase aromaticity and surface area, while slower heating rates improve carbon yield.
tp.step2.detail: Activation with KOH, K₂CO₃, or CO₂ expands pore networks from ~5 m²/g to over 3,000 m²/g. Elemental composition (CHNS-O) governs surface chemistry: high C content ensures stability, while N/O functional groups enhance CO₂ chemisorption affinity.
tp.step3.detail: CO₂ adsorption estimated using 3 parallel methods: statistical DB lookup (1,263 records), Ridge approximation, and a trained sklearn ML pipeline (KNN → SVR). Results shown side-by-side with agreement indicator — divergence flags limited data or model uncertainty.

th.desc: Thailand produces over 60 million tonnes of agricultural residue annually. BiocharHub maps the highest-potential feedstocks to their known biochar performance characteristics.
th.bottomDesc: {points} experimental data points across {species} biomass species, 6 activation methods, and {experiments} unique isotherm experiments — available for AI-driven prediction.
feedstock.riceHusk.note: Rice husk is high in silica; co-pyrolysis or ash retention can produce Si‑doped biochar that may enhance CO₂ affinity under certain activation conditions. Performance depends on activation method and pyrolysis temperature — see the cited studies for experimental details.
feedstock.cornStraw.note: Corn straw is cellulose-rich; experimental records show KOH activation often yields the highest measured CO₂ uptakes. Optimal adsorption performance is sensitive to activation protocol and high-temperature treatments — consult the cited studies for procedural details and uptake ranges.
feedstock.cassava.note: Cassava rhizome is starchy with relatively low ash content, producing high biochar yields that are attractive for soil amendment and carbon storage. These biochars balance yield and stability, making them suitable for agricultural applications where mass yield matters.
feedstock.coffee.note: Spent coffee grounds are nitrogen-rich feedstocks; K₂CO₃ activation commonly produces micropore-dominated biochars useful for selective CO₂/N₂ separation and applications requiring high microporosity. Performance depends on activation and thermal history.
flow.step1.label: Sustainable Feedstock
flow.step1.subtitle: Agricultural Waste
flow.step1.short: Agri-waste such as rice husk, corn straw, and coffee grounds are collected — materials that would otherwise be burned or landfilled.
flow.step1.heading: Step 1 — Sustainable Feedstock Collection
flow.step1.body: Thailand produces large quantities of agricultural residue annually. Rather than open‑field burning, selected feedstocks (e.g., rice husk, corn straw, cassava residues, spent coffee grounds) can be diverted to controlled biochar production for soil amendment and carbon storage.
flow.step2.label: Thermochemical Conversion
flow.step2.subtitle: Pyrolysis (300–900°C)
flow.step2.short: Biomass is heated to 300–900°C in an oxygen-limited environment, preserving carbon in a stable, porous solid matrix.
flow.step2.heading: Step 2 — Pyrolysis & Thermochemical Conversion
flow.step2.body: Pyrolysis thermochemically converts biomass into biochar, bio‑oil, and syngas (typical conditions 300–900°C). Temperature, heating rate, and residence time strongly influence yield, porosity, and surface chemistry — parameters captured in the 44Database.
flow.step3.label: Biochar Enrichment
flow.step3.subtitle: Chemical / Physical Activation
flow.step3.short: Activation with KOH, K₂CO₃, or CO₂ gas dramatically expands internal pore networks, yielding BET surface areas up to 3,157 m²/g.
flow.step3.heading: Step 3 — Activation & Pore Engineering
flow.step3.body: Activation (chemical or physical) increases surface area and pore volume by creating micropores and mesopores. Chemical agents (e.g., KOH, K₂CO₃) and physical activation (CO₂, steam) are common; combined methods often yield the highest BET values recorded in the database.
flow.step4.label: Permanent Carbon Sink
flow.step4.subtitle: CO₂ Adsorption & Sequestration
flow.step4.short: The engineered biochar captures CO₂ from flue gas or air at capacities up to 7.5 mmol/g — locking carbon away for centuries.
flow.step4.heading: Step 4 — CO₂ Capture & Permanent Sequestration
flow.step4.body: Activated biochar can capture CO₂ via physical adsorption and chemisorption; top reported uptakes vary by sample and test conditions. When applied to soils, biochar contributes to long‑term carbon storage and soil improvement. Refer to the Scientific References for measurement details and persistence estimates.

kc.fact1.title: What is Biochar?
kc.fact1.body: Biochar is a carbon‑rich solid produced by heating biomass (agricultural residues, wood, or other organic materials) under limited oxygen in a process called pyrolysis. It is engineered to retain stable carbon while developing a porous structure and surface chemistry that can improve soil fertility, retain water and nutrients, and act as an adsorbent for pollutants. Standard terminology and measurement approaches are discussed in the Scientific References.
kc.fact2.title: Why CO₂ Adsorption?
kc.fact2.body: Activated biochar develops a highly porous structure with surface areas up to 3,157 m²/g — comparable to half a football field per gram. This makes it exceptionally effective at capturing CO₂ molecules from flue gases and the atmosphere.
kc.fact3.title: Soil & Agriculture
kc.fact3.body: When applied to soil, biochar can improve water-holding capacity, reduce nutrient leaching, and modify microbial communities to support plant growth. Effects depend on feedstock, production conditions, and application rate; field trials in Thailand show yield and resilience benefits for rice in saline or degraded soils (see Scientific References for trial details).
kc.fact4.title: Carbon Sequestration
kc.fact4.body: Biochar is highly recalcitrant — its carbon resists decomposition for hundreds to thousands of years. Applying 1 tonne of biochar to soil can sequester approximately 2.5–3 tonnes of CO₂-equivalent, making it a viable negative-emission technology.

soc.heading: Biochar Society
soc.desc: Profiles of key organisations involved in research, standards, and deployment of biochar across Thailand. Visit their pages for publications, guidance, and programmes.
soc.org.mtec.desc: National Metal and Materials Technology Center — leads the NZE Biochar Programme, developing biochar standards and carbon-credit frameworks for Thailand.
soc.org.nstda.desc: National Science and Technology Development Agency — umbrella organisation for MTEC, BIOTEC, NANOTEC, ENTEC; funds and coordinates biochar research nationwide.
soc.org.biochar.desc: Multi-stakeholder consortium connecting researchers, farmers, and policymakers to accelerate biochar adoption in Thai agriculture and carbon markets.
soc.org.kasetsart.desc: Thailand's leading agricultural university — active biochar field trials across rice, sugarcane, and cassava systems; key partner in soil carbon research.
soc.org.tgo.desc: TGO manages Thailand's carbon credit registry (T-VER) and voluntary emission reduction programmes, including soil carbon and biochar-based credits.
soc.org.doa.desc: Thailand's Department of Agriculture oversees soil amendment standards and approves biochar products for agricultural use under national guidelines.
